items.title: 71542_Bill Coleman autobiographical manuscript
items.q: if you take a good negro band like Count Basie, it has a natural emotion in the way it plays. I believe we learnt that emotion in the Churches.

ctx.x: One Sunday, there was a parade passing on 9th street, and the bands interested me to the point where I decided to follow one, and must have been miles away from home when I decided I had better return. I had never been so far away from those front steps alone and did not know where I was. But I remembered the streets that I had followed the band, and eventually arrived home, happy to discover that I had not been missed by my mother and Aunt Mary. That was a beautiful Sunday, because I heard some music, something…

Looking back, I realize now that that kind of parade music was a basis for Jazz. That was how many Jazz players learned the harmonic connections. The rhythm came from the Churches. When I was about twelve years old, there used to be meetings of the "Holy Rollies", In the yard of a big house right on the corner near where we lived. They used to clap their hands, and the preacher was a wonderful tap dancer. He could really whip up the congregation with his rhythm. My mother was a Baptist, and we were all made to go…

I was going to school on 9th Street which was near where I lived and I had a playmate who was blond and Irish. In Kentucky the white and negro children never played together. But that was not the case in Cincinnati because the schools were mixed at that time. This boy lived near me on 9th Street and his mother worked in a laundry a few blocks up from the school and she used to give us pennies now and then to buy candy. We used to fight with two Jewish boys who were twins and whose names I remember being Ike and…
